categories.summary: Wings, control surfaces and fins push along their surface normal once airspeed passes 15 m/s, with force proportional to rudder_surface_area (wings 8 to 120, control surfaces 10 to 70, fins 2 to 12). Control surfaces deflect about 45° each way, fins about 14.3°.

sections.title: Sizing
sections.body: rudder_surface_area: wings 8, 20, 40, 70, 120; control surfaces 10, 28, 70; control fins 2, 8, 12. The air force is proportional to this field, so at the same airflow, body mass and altitude the large control surface pushes 7 times as hard as the small one. The listed voxel count does not enter the equation.

sections.title: Deflection
sections.body: The game turns the input into an angle in radians. Control surfaces store 0.785398, about 45° each way, and fins 0.25, about 14.3°, so a fin is the finer, smaller-authority choice. Each update the surface moves toward the requested position. With full electrical supply it gets there in one update; a weak supply slows it, and no supply holds it.

sections.title: Stabilisers
sections.body: Reaction wheels carry force fields 10, 100 and 1000, a factor of ten per size; wire them to an aligned angular speed sensor.

sections.title: Air force
sections.body:
Wings, control surfaces and fins share one air routine. It pushes along the surface normal with force 24 × rudder_surface_area × P × B × (1 - immersion) × (airspeed - 15) × (normal airspeed + wing term). Airspeed is the surface's speed relative to the wind in m/s, and at 15 m/s or less there is no air force. P = (1 - 2.2413793e-05 × height)^5.3595023 is the altitude pressure ratio, 1 at sea level and 0 above 40000 m. B = min(0.00003 × body mass, 0.2), so the coefficient stops growing at a body mass of 6666.67.

Wing sections (rudder_type 1) add a wing term 3 × c^5 × g. c is the cosine between the direction of travel through the air and the wing's forward axis, the reverse of its dynamic_rotation_axes vector, and g rises from 0 at 15 m/s to 1 at 40 m/s. Travelling along that axis, the term lifts a wing even at zero angle of attack; travelling the other way removes it. Matching that axis to a visible mesh edge is an inference. Control surfaces and fins (rudder_type 0) have no wing term, so they push only when the air meets them at an angle.

The routine multiplies by its own constant 24 and does not read the shipped lift_force setting (0.25), so changing lift_force does not change this force.

sections.title: Lift and drag
sections.body:
The force is a single push along the normal. With angle of attack α between the airflow and the surface, lift is that force × cos α and drag is force × sin α. Plane resistance grows with airspeed × (airspeed - 15); the wing term grows with (airspeed - 15) × g. There is no stall angle, Reynolds-number term or separate skin drag in this routine.

Example: a small wing section (area 8) on a body of mass 1000 at 30 m/s and 10° angle of attack gets a normal force of 594.2, of which 585.1 is lift and 103.2 is drag.

sections.title: Force units and limit
sections.body:
The result is in the game's internal force units. Body mass is not calibrated to kilograms, so do not read it as newtons. The game queues the force once per update and the physics solver integrates it, so it is not multiplied by 60. Before it is applied its size is limited to 5 × S, where S is a per-vehicle scale passed in by the component dispatcher; area scaling is linear only below that limit.

Partly under water, the air force is scaled by 1 minus the immersion fraction and a separate water term takes over.

limitations: The force equations come from static decompilation of one build; the game was not run. How the game builds the cap scale S for craft joined by locked joints was not decoded, so forces near the cap are not predicted.
Which visible edge and editor arrow match positive deflection and the sign of the force was not checked in game.
Internal mass and force units are not calibrated to kilograms and newtons.
Reaction wheels are outside the air-force decode; their force fields are configuration only.

categories.summary: Buttons accept an external on/off input so several buttons can drive one output; the large keypad also emits a pulse on confirm.

sections.title: Wiring
sections.body: Chain buttons through External Input to unify outputs. Toggle buttons and lock buttons can set their default state in the properties.

limitations: Tooltip semantics only.

categories.summary: Monitors and HUDs draw on a logical grid of 32 pixels per block across their X and Z voxel bounds, from 32×32 on a Monitor 1x1 to 288×160 on a Monitor 9x5. Touch Output returns the screen size and two touch points in pixels.

sections.title: Wiring
sections.body: Feed Video Signal from a microcontroller or camera, connect Electric and turn Power Switch on. For a touchscreen, wire Touch Output to a composite input on the microcontroller that draws the screen and its video output back to Video Signal. While the screen is switched off, every Touch Output channel reads 0.

sections.title: Resolution
sections.body:
The game sets width = 32 × (voxel_max.x - voxel_min.x + 1) and height = 32 × (voxel_max.z - voxel_min.z + 1) from the definition's block bounds. The same size comes back from screen.getWidth() and screen.getHeight() in onDraw and on Touch Output number channels 1 and 2.

Sizes in pixels: Monitor 1x1 32×32, Monitor 1x2 64×32, Monitor 1x3 96×32, Monitor 2x2 64×64, Monitor 2x3 96×64, Monitor 3x3 96×96, Monitor 5x3 160×96, Monitor 9x5 288×160, HUD Small 32×32, HUD Large 96×96.

The listed voxel count and monitor_border do not change the pixel grid. The graphics quality setting scales the render target by 1, 2 or 4 after the size is stored, so it leaves the Lua and touch grid alone.

sections.title: Touch Output
sections.body:
Touch Output is a composite. Number channels 1 and 2 carry the width and height in pixels, 3 and 4 the X and Y of the first touch, and 5 and 6 the X and Y of the second. Boolean channels 1 and 2 are on while the first and second touch are pressed. Coordinates are whole pixels from the upper left, X to the right and Y down, accepted from 0 up to the width and height inclusive.

The screen tracks at most two touches at once and ignores a third. Releasing a touch clears only its flag and leaves its last X and Y on the channels, so check the flag before using a coordinate. The touch area is the screen face inset by monitor_border on each side, stretched over the pixel grid.

sections.title: Lua callbacks
sections.body: Read the channels with input.getNumber and input.getBool in onTick, which runs once per logic tick; screen functions do nothing there. Draw in onDraw, which runs whenever a monitor draws the script and can run several times when one script drives several monitors. Composite functions do nothing in onDraw. The shipped example reads number channels 3 and 4 and boolean channel 1 in onTick and draws the matching rectangle in onDraw.

limitations: Resolution and touch layout come from static analysis of one build and its shipped definitions; the game was not run and no touch was tested in game.

Still open: a fixed refresh rate in Hz and the delay from a touch to the next drawn frame. onDraw follows monitor rendering rather than the 60-per-second component update, and the draw scheduling, culling and caching were outside this pass.
Still open: which player or input event takes each touch slot, and how HUD hits reach the touch setter.

categories.summary: Battery capacity is electric_charge_capacity (1 : 8 : 160 across sizes). electric_magnitude is a per-component multiplier on charge: a motor pays electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1 per unit of speed step, and a generator earns the same product per unit of speed it removes.

sections.title: Storage
sections.body: The electric-node initialiser copies electric_charge_capacity straight into the node: 1600, 12800 and 256000 for the small, medium and large battery. A large battery stores 160 times a small one. Batteries also have a Charge Level property from 0 to 100 that sets the stored charge when the vehicle spawns.

sections.title: What electric_magnitude does
sections.body:
The field is read at definition+0x1420 by six instructions in this build, and the formula differs per component. In the electric component update, a motor (electric_type 0) asks the network for |Δ| × electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1, where Δ is the speed step it wants this update. A generator (electric_type 1) deposits electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1 × |ω| × min(|ω| ÷ 560, 0.25). In both cases the speed change itself does not involve electric_magnitude. The field only sets how much charge a given speed change costs or earns, so for motors it works like an inverse efficiency (1.2, 1.1, 1.05) and for generators like an efficiency (0.6, 0.75, 0.85).

Generators get an internal buffer of 0.1 per listed voxel; solar cells and chargers get 0.01. No direct electric_magnitude read was found for batteries, breakers, relays, solar cells or chargers in this update; reads through differently computed pointers were not covered.

sections.title: Other components that reuse the field
sections.body: The field is not a global efficiency. A routine inferred to update classic engines (field value 1.2) uses it as a starter cost factor: max(5 − speed, 0) × engine_max_force × (an unidentified component value) ÷ 2000 × electric_magnitude × 0.1. The modular starter (0.2) requests max(5 − crank speed, 0) × electric_magnitude × engine_max_force × 0.1. The modular alternator (0.05) uses the generator formula with an extra 0.1. A branch inferred to handle jet turbines (field value 0.025) deposits |ω| × electric_magnitude × min(ω ÷ 10000, 0.02) when that is positive, with no force term. The modular clutch, drive belt and temperature sensor carry values (1, 1, 0.05) that none of the six reads uses; the scan covers only direct +0x1420 operands.

sections.title: Supply and settings
sections.body: Motors and both starters draw through the same helper. It removes min(a × request, network charge) and returns the supplied fraction, where a = max(0, (300 − n) ÷ 300) × q comes from two node fields whose meaning was not recovered. A motor's step is scaled by that fraction, so starving it slows acceleration without changing the cost per unit of step. With infinite_batteries on, the helper returns 1 and takes nothing. Generators deposit regardless of that setting.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Component updates run 60 times per simulated second, so 60 × the charge per update is the charge per simulated second, in internal units. The speed unit of ω and the shaft-link model were not recovered, so charge cannot yet be turned into charge per unit of work. The shipped realtime file sets electric_consumption_scale to 0.01, but the release binary does not contain that name.

limitations: Electric units are internal; no conversion to joules or watts was recovered.
ω is the component's internal speed state; how it maps to the RPS port and how the shaft link exchanges speed were not decoded.
Static analysis only.

categories.summary: Self-contained diesel engines differ by an engine_max_force field of 20000, 60000 and 200000; their runtime curves were not decoded, unlike the modular engine.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Throttle takes 0 to 1; the Starter input spins the engine with electricity until it runs. Fuel, air, cold and hot coolant, and exhaust each have their own connection.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: engine_max_force is 20000 for the small, 60000 for the medium and 200000 for the large diesel engine; the turbine engine has 100000. These are definition values whose use in the classic engine code was not traced.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Torque and fuel use against throttle for each engine; temperature rise per throttle level.

limitations: The classic engine update was not decompiled; prefer the modular engine article for recovered formulas.

categories.summary: Each connected pipe network is one 40 L compartment; pumps add a pressure bias, which caps equal-pressure flow at 200 L/s for the small electric pump and 400 L/s for the large one; tanks drift toward ambient temperature; fluid meters use one channel per fluid type.

sections.title: Moving fluid
sections.body:
Every connected run of ordinary pipe is one network compartment of volume 4, 40 L, however many pipe blocks it spans. For clean water its pressure is 15 × the stored amount, 60 when full. Each update the network shares its fluid and free room among the demands its ports set on the previous update, and each port then moves at most half its demand.

A pump adds its bias to the pressure difference. Electric pumps use electrical supply × pump_pressure × Max Power, impeller pumps 4 × |RPS| × pump_pressure, and the modular engine fluid pump its own shaft speed. At equal pressure the move is at most min(bias, 20) ÷ 30 amount per update: 200 L/s for the small electric pump (pump_pressure 10), 400 L/s for the large one (100), and no pump exceeds 400 L/s. The flow readout shows 1 amount per update as 600 L/s, 10 L per amount. The manual pump (pump_pressure 3) was not traced.

sections.title: Temperature carried with fluid
sections.body: Fluid arriving in a compartment is mixed by the compartment's amount after the move: T = (A' × T + q × T_donor) ÷ (A' + q). So 1 unit at 20 °C receiving 0.5 at 100 °C ends at 40 °C, not the 46.7 °C of ordinary mixing. Below 0.01 amount per update, radiator, manifold and two-way pump ports also exchange temperature directly at a rate of up to 0.1 ÷ volume per update, so heat crosses a port even with no net flow.

sections.title: Storage and temperature
sections.body: Tanks keep their contents' temperature and drift toward the surrounding temperature by 0.001 per update. At 60 updates per simulated second that leaves 0.942 of the gap after one second, a time constant of 16.7 s. The fluid spawner fills custom tanks; gases are spawned compressed at 60 atm.

sections.title: Identifying fluids
sections.body: The liquid and gas meters share one composite layout: 1 water, 2 diesel, 3 jet fuel, 4 air, 5 CO2, 6 oil, 7 seawater, 8 steam, 9 slurry, 10 saturated slurry, 11 oxygen, 12 nitrogen, 13 hydrogen. Air is reported as the sum of oxygen, carbon dioxide and nitrogen.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Whether the realtime damping values (0.99 gas, 0.9999 liquid) are used by this build. Compare Flow Rate in game with the recovered bounds; pipe length should not change it, because a network's volume does not grow with its length.

limitations: The network builder was traced for ordinary pipes only; hoses, tanks, open compartments, special connectors and the manual pump were not. Multiphase fluids, filters and sea water are outside the recovered clean-water model.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

categories.summary: Exchangers equalise two compartments by a fixed fraction per update weighted by how much fluid each side holds; radiators cool toward the surroundings and gain up to three times their passive rate from an electric fan or airflow.

sections.title: How the game moves heat
sections.body:
The fluid-component update gives every exchanger two internal compartments, A and B. Each update A moves toward B by 0.03·qB/(qA+qB) of the temperature gap and B moves toward A by 0.03·qA/(qA+qB), so heat is conserved and the gap shrinks by a constant fraction regardless of variant. The q terms are capacity values taken from the fluid inside each compartment. The fraction itself does not depend on the variant, so any size advantage must come through q or through-flow; it is plausible that larger variants hold more fluid, but their compartment volumes were not recovered, so that advantage is inferred, not shown.

Both compartments also leak toward the surrounding temperature by 0.001 per update. Radiators use a separate rule: the compartment moves toward the surrounding temperature by 0.003 × (1 + fan), with the fan term clamped to 0…2.

sections.title: Per-second rates
sections.body: Component updates run 60 times per simulated second. The fractions compound, so they are not multiplied by 60. With constant coefficients and nothing else acting, one simulated second leaves 0.161 of the gap between an exchanger's two compartments (time constant 0.547 s), 0.942 of a gap to fixed ambient through the leak alone (16.7 s), 0.835 of a passive radiator's gap to fixed ambient (5.55 s) and 0.581 at the full radiator multiplier of 3 (1.84 s). Through-flow and changing temperatures need the full model stepped 60 times per second.

sections.title: Practical setup
sections.body: Connect both ports of a side. The exchanger pushes fluid through a side only when its In and Out ports are both connected, and a radiator cools only when both of its fluid ports are connected. A radiator outside any enclosed compartment counts relative airflow as fan, reaching the maximum term at an air speed of 80 in the game's speed units (2 × 40). Inside a compartment that bonus is skipped and the reference temperature is the compartment's.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: The unit and per-fluid weighting of the q capacity terms and the filter applied to the surrounding-temperature sample (refreshed every 16 updates, 0.267 simulated seconds) were not recovered. Measure exchanger outlet temperatures at fixed flow to see how through-flow changes the isolated per-second figures.

limitations: Native findings come from static decompilation of one build; no in-game measurement was made.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.
The compartment volume of each exchanger variant was not recovered, so the size advantage cannot be stated as a ratio.

categories.summary: Storage units recharge stored equipment from vehicle power; tooltips give concrete limits such as 230 m diving depth for 10 minutes, scuba 40 m for 2 minutes and 500 m handheld radio range.

sections.title: Equipment limits
sections.body: Diving gear reaches 230 m with 10 minutes of air; scuba reaches 40 m with 2 minutes. Handheld radios and remotes use frequencies 0~8 with 500 m effective range. Firefighting and hazmat gear absorb 95% of fire or radiation damage.

limitations: Tooltip statements only.

categories.summary: Modular jets need electric power to start the compressor, combust once internal pressure is high enough, and make thrust proportional to internal RPS; the thrust spoiler takes 0 (none) to 1 (full reduction).

sections.title: Start-up and control
sections.body: Power and enable the compressor, feed jet fuel to the combustion chamber with throttle 0 to 1, and use the spoiler for reverse-free thrust control. The rotating exhaust vectors within −0.5 to 0.5 turns; the afterburner adds thrust for more fuel.

limitations: Jet simulation code was not decoded.

categories.summary: Logic gates document their edge cases precisely: divide by zero outputs 0 with an error flag, thresholds are inclusive, trigonometry uses turns, SR latches favour Reset and JK flip-flops toggle.

sections.title: Edge cases worth knowing
sections.body: Divide outputs 0 and raises Error on division by zero. Threshold is on when lower ≤ x ≤ upper. Greater Than is off when A equals B. Sin, cos and tan take turns; asin, acos and atan return turns; invalid input gives 0. An SR latch with both inputs on resets; a JK flip-flop toggles. Delay and Blinker timers restart when their input changes or switches off. The PID controller clears its stored values when Active is off.

limitations: Tooltip semantics; the logic evaluator was not decompiled.

categories.summary: Powered pivots, hinges, turrets and sliders expose Speed, Max Power and a Gear Ratio of 1:1 to 1:32; robotic joints are limited to 0.25 turns either way while velocity joints and turret rings turn continuously.

sections.title: Joint properties
sections.body: Multibody components whose definition flags include 0x100 get a Max Power slider shown as a percentage and a Gear Ratio selector with 1:1, 1:2, 1:4, 1:8, 1:16 and 1:32. Robotic and velocity types additionally show a Speed slider.

sections.title: Choosing a joint
sections.body: Robotic pivots and hinges seek a target inside ±0.25 turns and report Current Rotation in that range. Velocity pivots and turret rings rotate continuously at the commanded speed, report rotation in turns, and stop at an input of 0. Turret rings also extend a sealed volume through the ring.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: How the gear ratio trades speed for holding torque and what Max Power scales were not recovered numerically; measure with a torque meter on a torque-capable joint.

limitations: The numeric effect of Gear Ratio and Max Power was not decoded.
Static analysis only.

categories.summary: Recovered cylinder code gives a concrete tuning target: keep the air:fuel ratio near 13.6–14.0, keep the crank below 60 RPS, keep manifolds under 115 °C and give the exhaust room.

sections.title: Combustion window
sections.body: Each cylinder computes a fuel term (RPS × 4e-6 × voxels × fuel throttle) and an intake term (RPS × 2.8e-6 × voxels ÷ 60 × air throttle × pressure factor). At 60 updates per simulated second the fuel term is RPS × 0.00024 × voxels × fuel throttle per second. The displayed air:fuel ratio is intake × 600 ÷ fuel, so with equal throttles and no boost it reads 7. Combustion happens only when the ratio lies between 12 − 2t and 16 + 4t, where t is manifold temperature ÷ 100 clamped to 0…1. Within the window the mixture factor 1 − 2(s − 0.6)² peaks at an air:fuel ratio of 13.6 cold and 14.0 when the manifold is at or above 100 °C.

sections.title: Speed, heat and damage
sections.body: Fuel admission is cut above 60 RPS, so cylinders act as a hard rev limiter. Speed efficiency falls from 1 at standstill to 0.5 at 50 RPS. Burning fuel heats the manifold group (gain 6000 ÷ heat capacity); above 115 °C, with engine overheating enabled, the cylinder takes damage every 300 updates (5 simulated seconds), and torque gain drops from 80000 to 40000 once damaged.

sections.title: Assembly
sections.body: Crank inertia is the sum of engine_max_force over the assembly: a 1x1 crank block adds 0.7 while flywheels add 150, 600 and 2400. Inertia divides every torque impulse, so flywheels smooth speed and make starting slower. The starter only pushes while the crank is below 5 RPS.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Compartment pressure units and the units of manifold heat and coolant transfer were not recovered; measure RPS response and temperatures in game to calibrate these.

limitations: All engine formulas are reconstructed from static decompilation of build f9206d85…; they were not checked in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.
Throttle offsets 0x88 and 0x90 are attributed to the fuel and air manifolds from the oxygen/diesel caps applied to them; the manifold write path was only partially traced.

categories.summary: This catch-all holds sensors, radios, lights, fluid fittings, connectors, winches, doors and tools; the most useful hard numbers are ranges, which the definitions confirm: v2 radios 100 m to 20 km with legacy radios configured identically, and radar ranges from 5000 to 500000 m.

sections.title: Radio ranges
sections.body: rx_range equals the tooltip's ground-level range on every v2 radio (100, 1000, 4000, 20000) and on the directional antennas (8000000, 10000000). The legacy radios carry the same rx_range values as their v2 counterparts, so expect the same ranges.

sections.title: Radar and sonar ranges
sections.body: radar_range matches the stated range for the basic radars (5000, 20000, 50000), sonars (3000, 1000), advanced sonars (60000, 100000, 200000) and the fish finder (100). The advanced radars without a stated range carry 60000 (radar), 500000 (AWACS), 200000 (dish), 100000 (phalanx) and 20000 (missile).

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Detection probability against target size and FOV for the advanced radars; radio signal strength against distance.

limitations: Range fields are configuration; detection and signal models were not decoded.
Unrelated definitions carry serialized default ranges; only sensor and radio definitions are interpreted here.

categories.summary: Propellers and rotors carry a force_emitter_max_force field that ranks variants (marine 20000 to 200000, rotors 40000 to 200000); marine propellers work only underwater and rotors lose force underwater.

sections.title: Variant ranking
sections.body: force_emitter_max_force: marine propellers 20000, 100000 and 200000; pitchable propellers 20000, 80000 and 160000; helicopter rotors 40000 and 200000; heavy rotors 120000 and 200000; ducted fans 2000 and 10000. Helicopter and through-drive rotors also carry force_emitter_efficiency 1.25 where most other emitters carry 1.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Marine propellers and the azimuth thruster operate only underwater; helicopter rotors produce less force underwater. Solid rocket boosters burn once; a slower burn-rate setting lasts longer but gives less thrust.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Whether force_emitter_max_force is a thrust cap and how RPS maps to thrust were not recovered; measure thrust against RPS with a fixed test rig.

limitations: Force-emitter fields are configuration; their runtime use was not decoded.

categories.summary: Pilot seats expose four axes from −1 to 1, six hotkeys, look angles in turns and a composite with fixed channels (on/off 31 trigger, 32 occupied; values 1–4 axes, 9–10 look).

sections.title: Composite layout
sections.body: On/Off 1 and up carry hotkeys, 31 the trigger and 32 occupancy; values 1–4 carry the axes and 9–10 the look direction. The HOTAS seat adds axes 5–8 and up to 48 hotkeys.

limitations: Port descriptions only.

categories.summary: Steam power chains a coal firebox, boiler, piston or turbine and condenser; duct sizes carry capacity fields 42.1875, 195.3125 and 351.5625.

sections.title: Chain
sections.body: The firebox consumes one coal to ignite and heats coolant; the boiler turns that heat into steam and should be throttled to hold steam pressure; pistons need pressure alternated between their couplings by piston position; the condenser must stay cooled.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Heat output per coal, boiler evaporation rate and piston torque against pressure.

limitations: Steam simulation code was not decoded.

categories.summary: Weight blocks shift the centre of mass; keels resist roll and lateral slip while submerged, letting sails drive a boat across or into the wind.

sections.title: Keels and skis
sections.body: Keels are the counterpart to sails; skis slide lengthwise and grip laterally.

limitations: Tooltip statements; keel force code was not decoded.

categories.summary: Gearboxes switch between two ratios picked from a fixed list of eight, including a 1:-1 reverse, and need electricity to change ratio.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Gearboxes use torque_component_type 1. Gear Switch off applies the Ratio Off selection, on applies Ratio On. The gearbox only changes ratio while it has electrical availability; without power it keeps the last ratio. Each change draws electricity.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Both ratios are chosen from eight fixed options, not typed numbers: 1:-1, 1:1, 6:5, 3:2, 9:5, 2:1, 5:2 and 3:1. Internally they become the multipliers -1, 1, 0.8333333, 0.6666667, 0.5555556, 0.5, 0.4 and 0.33333334; the coupling stores the reciprocal. 1:-1 reverses direction without changing speed.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Which side (RPS A or RPS B) turns faster for an N:1 option, and how much torque the coupling transmits before slipping, need an in-game torque meter test.

limitations: Ratio orientation (which port is the faster side) was not established.
Static analysis only.

categories.summary: Autocannon drums hold 100, 200 or 500 rounds and machine-gun boxes 100 or 400; barrels add accuracy and recoil, muzzle brakes cut recoil.

sections.title: Ammunition
sections.body: Drums hold one caliber each; machine-gun boxes take only kinetic, armour-piercing and incendiary rounds and must be refilled by hand. Autocannons need electricity to feed from belts or drums.

sections.title: Barrel tuning
sections.body: Barrel extensions increase accuracy but also recoil (some heavy and rotary barrels add weight instead); a muzzle brake at the end reduces recoil. Fuse Timer sets a delay in seconds for high-explosive and fragmentation rounds.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Spread and recoil per barrel extension, projectile velocity and damage.

limitations: Ballistics were not decoded.

categories.summary: Wheel radius fields (0.35 to 1.05 for road wheels) set ground speed per RPS if they are rolling radii in metres; track wheels only form tracks with matching wheels in line.

sections.title: Choosing a size
sections.body: Road wheels carry wheel_radius 0.35, 0.58, 0.85 and 1.05. The distance sensor tooltip equates one metre with four blocks, so if this is a rolling radius in metres the no-slip speed is 2π × radius × RPS: about 2.2 m/s per RPS for the smallest and 6.6 m/s per RPS for the largest.

sections.title: Tracks
sections.body: Track wheels form a track only with wheels of the same size and orientation placed in line on the same body; at least one drive wheel must receive power.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Confirm the radius unit with a linear speed sensor at known RPS; measure slip under load.

limitations: The metre interpretation of wheel_radius is unverified; speed figures are no-slip geometry, not measurements.

categories.summary: Windows are geometry pieces; their definitions describe shape and placement only, and no window-specific behaviour was recovered.

sections.title: Placement
sections.body: Flat windows sit flush with walls; angled and corner pieces close gaps between angled windows.

limitations: No window-specific behaviour was located.

families.summary: Equalises two gas compartments by 0.03 of the gap per update, weighted by gas capacity on each side.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Case 0x11 uses the gas capacity helper for both sides; each side passes gas only with both its In and Out ports connected.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: The per-update rule is the same as for the other exchangers: 0.03 of the gap, weighted by the opposite side's share of capacity, plus a 0.001 drift toward ambient. Without through-flow, 0.161 of the gap remains after one simulated second.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: How gas pressure affects the capacity term was not recovered; measure the exchanger at different manifold pressures.

findings.label: Exchanger step fraction

limitations: The gas capacity weighting was not recovered.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Equalises an air compartment with a liquid compartment by 0.03 of the gap per update, weighted by each side's fluid capacity.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Case 0x12 of the fluid-component update treats side A as gas (Air In/Air Out) and side B as liquid (Fluid In/Fluid Out). Fluid only flows through a side whose In and Out ports are both connected; the A/B exchange itself runs whenever the two compartments together hold more than 0.001 capacity units.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: Per update, A moves toward B by 0.03·qB/(qA+qB) and B toward A by 0.03·qA/(qA+qB). Both sides use the same rule; only the capacity helper differs by fluid type. When the liquid side's capacity is much larger than the air side's, the air moves toward the liquid temperature by close to 0.03 of the gap per update while the liquid barely changes; with similar capacities each side moves about half that. The fraction is capped at 0.03 per update, so closing a large gap takes many updates and depends on fresh fluid flowing through. With no through-flow and no ambient leak, 0.161 of the gap remains after one simulated second (60 updates).

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: All five variants share the same code path and the same 0.03 fraction. If larger variants hold more fluid in their compartments (plausible but not established, because compartment volumes were not recovered), q and the heat moved per update would rise with size.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Temp A and Temp B read the internal compartments, so they show how close the two sides are, not inlet temperatures. Both compartments also drift toward the surrounding temperature by 0.001 per update, so an idle exchanger slowly settles to ambient: the leak alone has a time constant of 16.7 simulated seconds.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Measure Temp A/Temp B against flow rate to calibrate how fast fluid passing through refreshes each compartment, and compare variants at equal flow to quantify the size effect.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Force scales linearly with rudder_surface_area, so medium and large fins make 4 and 6 times the force of the small one under the same conditions. Fins have smaller area and deflection than control surfaces, suiting fine trim.

sections.title: Air force
sections.body: Fins use the same routine as control surfaces, with rudder_type 0 and no wing term: force = 24 × area × P × B × (1 - immersion) × (airspeed - 15) × normal airspeed, above 15 m/s.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Force scales linearly with rudder_surface_area, so medium and large surfaces make 2.8 and 7 times the force of the small one under the same conditions. All sizes share the 45° limit and the -1 to 1 Rotation input.

sections.title: Air force
sections.body: Control surfaces have rudder_type 0, so there is no wing term: force = 24 × area × P × B × (1 - immersion) × (airspeed - 15) × normal airspeed, above 15 m/s. A surface edge-on to the airflow makes no force.

sections.title: Deflection speed
sections.body: Moving the surface draws electricity in proportion to the requested change. With full supply it reaches the requested angle in one update; with partial supply it moves part of the way.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Throttle takes 0 to 1; the Starter input spins the engine with electricity until it runs. Fuel, air, cold and hot coolant, and exhaust each have their own connection.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: engine_max_force is 20000 for the small, 60000 for the medium and 200000 for the large diesel engine; the turbine engine has 100000. These are definition values whose use in the classic engine code was not traced.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Torque and fuel use against throttle for each engine; temperature rise per throttle level.

families.summary: Pushes fluid with a bias of electrical supply × pump_pressure × Max Power; at equal pressure the small pump moves at most 200 L/s and the large one 400 L/s.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: The pump needs power and the On/Off signal. Each update it calls the two-port solver with bias = electrical supply × pump_pressure × Max Power. Supply is the share of its electricity request it receives, 1 with unlimited electricity, and Max Power defaults to 100 %. The pump is one-way: it never pushes fluid backward. It holds no fluid itself; its ports connect straight to the pipe networks. Off or damaged, it passes nothing. It requests 0.001 × Max Power electricity per update, the same for both sizes.

sections.title: Flow
sections.body:
At equal pressure on both sides the move is at most min(bias, 20) ÷ 30 amount per update. That is 200 L/s for the small pump and 400 L/s for the large one at full power. The large pump's bias reaches 20 at 20 % Max Power, so it keeps the 400 L/s bound down to that setting. The small pump reaches 200 L/s only at full power, though pressure from upstream can push more through it.

These are bounds. Real flow falls with fill, backpressure and other ports on the same network. In the report's reference loop with one 3x3 radiator, the small pump settled at 42.6 L/s and the large one at 165.5 L/s. The cooling capacity calculator's finite-flow mode steps such loops.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: pump_pressure 100 against 10 gives the large pump a tenfold bias, but the solver caps any bias above 20, so at full power its bound is twice the small pump's, not ten times.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Compare Flow Rate in game with the bounds above and with the finite-flow estimate for the same loop.

families.summary: Cools its fluid toward the surrounding temperature at 0.003 × (1 + fan) per update; the electric fan can triple the passive rate.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Cooling runs only while both Fluid A and Fluid B are connected. The fan term is 2 × the electrical availability while Fan On/Off is on and power is present; each powered update also draws 0.001 units through the shared electricity helper, 0.06 units per simulated second.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: Cooling multiplier = 1 + fan, with fan clamped to 0…2, so a fully powered fan gives three times the passive rate. Mounted outside an enclosed compartment, relative airflow counts as fan as speed ÷ 40, so a fast vehicle reaches full cooling without power. The term alone leaves 0.835 of the gap to ambient after one simulated second at multiplier 1 and 0.581 at multiplier 3.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Both sizes run the same rule and fraction. The compartment volume equals the listed voxels: 9 for the 3x3 and 25 for the 5x5, at 10 L per unit. The larger radiator therefore cools more stored water per update, if the pump keeps it filled.

sections.title: Flow through the radiator
sections.body:
Each update the radiator exchanges with its Fluid A network, then its Fluid B network, then cools. Arriving water is mixed by the radiator's amount after the move, and below 0.01 amount per update a direct exchange also moves temperature through the ports. Its volume is capacity: in a pumped loop it need not stay full, and its water settles cooler than the coolant manifold.

For one radiator fed at a fixed inlet temperature with flow q and stored water A, the outlet sits q ÷ (k × A + (1 + k) × q) of the way from ambient to the inlet, with k = 0.003 × (1 + fan). With 9 units of water, 200 L/s and a full fan that is 83.90 °C out for 100 °C in at 20 °C ambient, a 16.10 °C drop. The cooling capacity calculator's finite-flow mode steps whole loops.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Measure Temperature against fan state and airspeed to confirm the units of the airflow term and the surrounding-temperature reference.

limitations: The airflow quantity is read as relative air speed from the vector-length call it is derived from; its unit was not confirmed.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Each update the motor takes a speed step of at most 2 × |Throttle| and requests |step| × electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1 in charge: 0.24, 6.6 and 26.25 per unit of step for the small, medium and large motor.

sections.title: How the update works
sections.body: With s = Throttle clamped to −1…1, the step is Δ = (20 × sign(s) − speed) × |s|, clamped to −2|s| … 2|s|. Δ is dropped when its sign differs from the throttle's, so a motor running faster than 20 in the throttle direction is not held back, while reversing the throttle drives it toward −20. At zero throttle it only coasts. The motor requests |Δ| × electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1, multiplies Δ by the fraction supplied, adds it, and then keeps 0.995 of its speed. With a shaft link it writes that speed and force_emitter_max_force into the link and takes the link's speed back. A damaged motor targets 0; the same step sign gate still applies.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: At the full-throttle step of 2, the small, medium and large motor request 0.48, 13.2 and 52.5 per update. While the step stays at that bound, that is 28.8, 792 and 3150 per simulated second; supply limits the actual draw. Per unit of force_emitter_max_force the cost is 0.12, 0.11 and 0.105, so if the shaft link weights speed by that force (the generator comparison makes the same assumption), the small motor pays 1.1429 times and the medium 1.0476 times what the large one pays for the same force-weighted speed change.

sections.title: What the cost tracks
sections.body: Charge scales with the speed step, not with speed × step. A given speed change costs the same at low and high shaft speed, so equal charge buys equal force-weighted speed change rather than equal mechanical work. Turning it into work needs the shaft-link model, which was not decoded.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Throttle limits the step, not the target speed: the target is always 20 in the motor's internal speed units. Without a shaft link the update settles at 19.9 at full throttle. At zero throttle an unlinked motor keeps 0.74 of its speed after one simulated second. Under load, a lower throttle mainly lowers the step and with it the draw. With infinite_batteries on, the draw helper supplies every request and takes no charge.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. families.summary: Two selectable ratios from a fixed list of eight; switching requires power.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Gearboxes use torque_component_type 1. Gear Switch off applies the Ratio Off selection, on applies Ratio On. The gearbox only changes ratio while it has electrical availability; without power it keeps the last ratio. Each change draws electricity.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Both ratios are chosen from eight fixed options, not typed numbers: 1:-1, 1:1, 6:5, 3:2, 9:5, 2:1, 5:2 and 3:1. Internally they become the multipliers -1, 1, 0.8333333, 0.6666667, 0.5555556, 0.5, 0.4 and 0.33333334; the coupling stores the reciprocal. 1:-1 reverses direction without changing speed.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Which side (RPS A or RPS B) turns faster for an N:1 option, and how much torque the coupling transmits before slipping, need an in-game torque meter test.

families.summary: Charge per update is electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1 × |ω| × min(|ω| ÷ 560, 0.25). The speed the generator removes does not depend on electric_magnitude, so 0.6, 0.75 and 0.85 act as conversion factors.

sections.title: How the update works
sections.body: The generator writes its speed and force_emitter_max_force into its shaft link and takes the link's speed ω back. With k = min(|ω| ÷ 560, 0.25), it deposits Q = electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1 × |ω| × k into the electric network and keeps (1 − k) of its speed; that loss is the load it puts on the shaft. Charge grows with the square of speed below |ω| = 140 and linearly above it. The update also writes 60 × Q to the slot where the battery keeps its Charge output, so Output most likely reads 60 × Q. Component updates run 60 times per simulated second, so 60 × Q is the charge the generator deposits per simulated second while ω holds steady.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Per unit of speed removed, the small, medium and large generator deposit 0.06, 2.25 and 10.625. Divided by force_emitter_max_force that is 0.06, 0.075 and 0.085, so for the same force-weighted speed removal the large generator yields 1.4167 times and the medium 1.25 times what the small one does. That comparison assumes the shaft link weights each part's speed by force_emitter_max_force, which matches how the parts write into it but was not decoded.

sections.title: Compared with motors and the alternator
sections.body: A motor driving a generator of the same size returns 0.5 (small), 0.6818 (medium) or 0.8095 (large) of the motor's charge for an equal force-weighted speed change, under the same assumption. At equal |ω| × k the modular alternator's coefficient is 0.05 against the small generator's 0.06.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Output is not labelled with a unit, and the charge unit itself has no recovered conversion to joules. Measure Output against shaft RPS per size to fix the unit of ω.

The shaft-link exchange and the unit of ω were not decoded; the force-weighted comparisons depend on that link.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: HUD Small draws 32×32 pixels and HUD Large 96×96. HUDs use the monitor component, with the same Touch Output channels.

sections.title: Resolution by size
sections.body:
The game sets width = 32 × (voxel_max.x - voxel_min.x + 1) and height = 32 × (voxel_max.z - voxel_min.z + 1) from the definition's block bounds. The same size comes back from screen.getWidth() and screen.getHeight() in onDraw and on Touch Output number channels 1 and 2.

Sizes in pixels: HUD Small 32×32, HUD Large 96×96.

HUDs have component type 43, the monitor type, so the same resolution routine and touch setter apply. Their definitions leave the Touch Output description empty; the channel layout below is the explanation.

The listed voxel count and monitor_border do not change the pixel grid. The graphics quality setting scales the render target by 1, 2 or 4 after the size is stored, so it leaves the Lua and touch grid alone.

sections.title: Touchscreen channels
sections.body:
Touch Output is a composite. Number channels 1 and 2 carry the width and height in pixels, 3 and 4 the X and Y of the first touch, and 5 and 6 the X and Y of the second. Boolean channels 1 and 2 are on while the first and second touch are pressed. Coordinates are whole pixels from the upper left, X to the right and Y down, accepted from 0 up to the width and height inclusive.

The screen tracks at most two touches at once and ignores a third. Releasing a touch clears only its flag and leaves its last X and Y on the channels, so check the flag before using a coordinate. The touch area is the screen face inset by monitor_border on each side, stretched over the pixel grid.

sections.title: Lua callbacks
sections.body: Read the channels with input.getNumber and input.getBool in onTick, which runs once per logic tick; screen functions do nothing there. Draw in onDraw, which runs whenever a monitor draws the script and can run several times when one script drives several monitors. Composite functions do nothing in onDraw. The shipped example reads number channels 3 and 4 and boolean channel 1 in onTick and draws the matching rectangle in onDraw.

sections.title: Wiring
sections.body: Feed Video Signal from a microcontroller or camera, connect Electric and turn Power Switch on. For a touchscreen, wire Touch Output to a composite input on the microcontroller that draws the screen and its video output back to Video Signal. While the screen is switched off, every Touch Output channel reads 0.

limitations: Resolution and touch layout come from static analysis of one build and its shipped definitions; the game was not run and no touch was tested in game.

Still open: a fixed refresh rate in Hz and the delay from a touch to the next drawn frame. onDraw follows monitor rendering rather than the 60-per-second component update, and the draw scheduling, culling and caching were outside this pass.
Still open: which player or input event takes each touch slot, and how HUD hits reach the touch setter.

families.summary: Shaft-driven pumps with bias 4 × |RPS| × pump_pressure (1 small, 9 standard); at equal pressure the small pump reaches the 400 L/s bound at 5 RPS and the standard one at 0.556 RPS.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: The impeller reads the speed of the shaft on its RPS port and pushes with bias 4 × |RPS| × pump_pressure. Spinning the shaft backward pushes the same way. Unlike the electric pumps it is two-way: backpressure can push fluid back through it, and at low flow it exchanges temperature between its two networks. The shaft port records a load request of 0.1 × pump_pressure; its torque unit was not established.

sections.title: Flow
sections.body: At equal pressure the move is at most min(bias, 20) ÷ 30 amount per update, 20 L/s per unit of bias up to 400 L/s. The small pump (pump_pressure 1) reaches that ceiling at 5 RPS and the standard one (9) at 0.556 RPS. These are bounds; backpressure, fill and other ports lower the real flow.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: They pump only while the shaft turns; compare variants with the Flow Rate output in L/s.

findings.label: Impeller flow bound
findings.value: small 20 × min(4 × |RPS|, 20) L/s, reached at 5 RPS; large 20 × min(36 × |RPS|, 20) L/s, reached at 0.556 RPS
findings.detail: Equal-pressure bound with b = 4 × |RPS| × pump_pressure (1 small, 9 large): q ≤ min(b, 20) ÷ 30 amount per update, 600 × that in L/s. The 400 L/s ceiling is reached at 20 ÷ 4 = 5 RPS for the small pump and 20 ÷ 36 = 0.556 RPS for the large one. Backpressure can make actual flow much lower or reverse it. Report: investigation/fluid-transport.md. findings.label: Equal-pressure pump flow bound
findings.value: min(max(b, 0), 20) ÷ 30 per update; small 200 L/s, large 400 L/s; 400 L/s absolute
findings.detail: With pipe networks of volume 4 on both ports at equal pressure and away from empty or full states, demand = (P_A - P_B + 2 × b) ÷ 30 and the move is at most half of it, so q ≤ min(max(b, 0), 20) ÷ 30 amount per update. The ±20 target band caps every listed pump at 2 ÷ 3 amount per update, 400 L/s. Small electric pump at full power, b = 10: 1 ÷ 3 per update, 20 amount per second, 200 L/s. Large, b = 100: 2 ÷ 3, 40 amount per second, 400 L/s. A small pump can exceed 200 L/s when upstream pressure helps it. These are bounds, not the flow a loop delivers; fill, backpressure and competing ports reduce it. Report: investigation/fluid-transport.md. findings.label: Pump target pressure band
findings.detail: The two-port solver forms z = P_A - P_B + bias, held at 0 or more for one-way pumps, and a target pressure from the window-weighted mean minus the bias, kept within this of the source pressure and within 0 to 60. findings.label: Recipient amount in temperature mixing
findings.value: post-transfer amount
findings.detail: After a port move the recipient's total (+0x40) is read after it has grown by the packet q, then q is added again for the divisor: T = (A' × T + q × T_donor) ÷ (A' + q), with A' the amount after the move. findings.value: small pump 42.6 L/s, coolant 107.2 °C, radiator 69.1 °C; large pump 165.5 L/s, coolant 101.4 °C, radiator 85.1 °C
findings.detail: Output of the report's 60 Hz fresh-water model, not a game measurement: pump, one 3x3 radiator (volume 9, fan 2), coolant manifold of a 3x3 cylinder group (volume 11.81), one pipe network of volume 4 between each pair, engine held at 115 °C, ambient 20 °C, pipes empty and radiator and manifold full at the start. The sail force is strongest when fully facing the wind to act as a parachute, but also has a strong force when facing slightly off a right-angle from the wind to act as a wing. A keel is recommended for sailboats to apply sail forces in a useful direction.

families.summary: Uses the same eight-option ratio list and power gate as the modular gearboxes; torque_gearbox_2 states a 4000 torque-difference limit.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Gearboxes use torque_component_type 1. Gear Switch off applies the Ratio Off selection, on applies Ratio On. The gearbox only changes ratio while it has electrical availability; without power it keeps the last ratio. Each change draws electricity.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Both ratios are chosen from eight fixed options, not typed numbers: 1:-1, 1:1, 6:5, 3:2, 9:5, 2:1, 5:2 and 3:1. Internally they become the multipliers -1, 1, 0.8333333, 0.6666667, 0.5555556, 0.5, 0.4 and 0.33333334; the coupling stores the reciprocal. 1:-1 reverses direction without changing speed.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Which side (RPS A or RPS B) turns faster for an N:1 option, and how much torque the coupling transmits before slipping, need an in-game torque meter test.

sections.title: Legacy definitions
sections.body: Both legacy definitions carry torque_component_type 1 and so share the modular gearbox code path; only torque_gearbox_2's tooltip states an operating limit of 4000 torque difference.

families.summary: Equalises two liquid compartments by 0.03 of the gap per update, weighted by liquid capacity on each side.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Case 0x10 uses the liquid capacity helper for both sides. Each side passes fluid only with both its In and Out ports connected.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: Per update the hotter compartment loses and the colder gains heat in proportion 0.03·q_other/(qA+qB), conserving the capacity-weighted temperature. Without through-flow the gap keeps 0.161 of its size after one simulated second (time constant 0.547 s). Throughput depends on how quickly flowing liquid replaces each compartment's contents.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: The 2x2 and 5x5 variants share the same fraction; a larger internal volume for the 5x5 would raise q, but the volumes were not recovered.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Compare outlet temperatures of both variants at equal pump flow.

families.summary: Burns diesel with manifold oxygen inside a temperature-dependent air:fuel window; best efficiency near ratio 13.6 cold and 14.0 hot, no fuel above 60 RPS.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: A cylinder produces torque only when the crank is above 2 RPS, its air:fuel ratio is inside the window 12 − 2t … 16 + 4t (t = manifold °C ÷ 100, clamped 0…1), and the crank is at or below 60 RPS. Fuel is capped by the diesel available in its fuel manifolds and intake by the oxygen in its air manifolds.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: Fuel per update = RPS × 4e-6 × listed voxels × fuel throttle, which is RPS × 0.00024 × listed voxels × fuel throttle per simulated second. Intake = RPS × 2.8e-6 × listed voxels ÷ 60 × air throttle × pressure factor, where the pressure factor rises from 1 to 2 with air-manifold pressure (scale 0.01). Efficiency = speed efficiency × mixture factor; speed efficiency = clamp(4(0.02·RPS + 0.5)/(0.02·RPS + 1)² − 1, 0, 1), and the mixture factor 1 − 2(s − 0.6)² peaks at the air:fuel ratio 13.6 cold, 14.0 hot. The displayed Stoichiometric value is 2s − 1, so aim for about 0.2.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: The cylinder code multiplies fuel and intake by the definition's listed voxel count: 1 for the 1x1, 27 for the 3x3 and 125 for the 5x5. At equal RPS and throttle a 3x3 cylinder therefore admits 27 times the fuel of a 1x1 and heats its manifolds correspondingly.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: With equal air and fuel throttles and no boost the ratio is 7, below the window, so the engine will not fire; reduce fuel throttle to roughly half of air throttle or add manifold pressure. Exhaust that cannot fit into the exhaust manifolds reduces torque and heat in proportion (Exhaust % in the inspection text). Above 115 °C with overheating enabled the cylinder accumulates damage every 300 updates, once per 5 simulated seconds; while damaged its torque gain halves from 80000 to 40000, and at a counter of 20 it stops producing torque.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Confirm the target ratio in game with the Air:Fuel Ratio inspection line; measure how manifold pressure units relate to the pressure factor; time the damage interval to check the 5-second period.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.
The fuel/air attribution of the two throttle offsets rests on the diesel and oxygen caps applied to them.
The counter at component offset 0x8 is read as damage because the overheat branch increments it (capped at 50); its other writers were not traced.

families.summary: Adds 150, 600 or 2400 to the crank inertia sum, against 0.7 for a 1x1 crank block; it smooths speed and slows starting.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: Every cylinder torque impulse is divided by the summed crank inertia. The flywheels also add the same amount to a second accumulator from engine_frictionless_force, whose use was not traced.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: The starter's coupling weights its own inertia (engine_max_force 0.5) against the crank inertia and only assists below 5 RPS, so a large flywheel noticeably lengthens cranking. Expect smaller RPS dips under load in exchange.

families.summary: Monitors draw 32 pixels per block of width and height, from 32×32 (Monitor 1x1) to 288×160 (Monitor 9x5). Touch Output reports that size and two touch points in pixels.

sections.title: Resolution by size
sections.body:
The game sets width = 32 × (voxel_max.x - voxel_min.x + 1) and height = 32 × (voxel_max.z - voxel_min.z + 1) from the definition's block bounds. The same size comes back from screen.getWidth() and screen.getHeight() in onDraw and on Touch Output number channels 1 and 2.

Sizes in pixels: Monitor 1x1 32×32, Monitor 1x2 64×32, Monitor 1x3 96×32, Monitor 2x2 64×64, Monitor 2x3 96×64, Monitor 3x3 96×96, Monitor 5x3 160×96, Monitor 9x5 288×160.

Follow the bounds, not the name: in Monitor 1x2, 1x3 and 2x3 the first number is the height in blocks, while 5x3 and 9x5 give the width first.

The listed voxel count and monitor_border do not change the pixel grid. The graphics quality setting scales the render target by 1, 2 or 4 after the size is stored, so it leaves the Lua and touch grid alone.

sections.title: Touchscreen channels
sections.body:
Touch Output is a composite. Number channels 1 and 2 carry the width and height in pixels, 3 and 4 the X and Y of the first touch, and 5 and 6 the X and Y of the second. Boolean channels 1 and 2 are on while the first and second touch are pressed. Coordinates are whole pixels from the upper left, X to the right and Y down, accepted from 0 up to the width and height inclusive.

The screen tracks at most two touches at once and ignores a third. Releasing a touch clears only its flag and leaves its last X and Y on the channels, so check the flag before using a coordinate. The touch area is the screen face inset by monitor_border on each side, stretched over the pixel grid.

sections.title: Lua callbacks
sections.body: Read the channels with input.getNumber and input.getBool in onTick, which runs once per logic tick; screen functions do nothing there. Draw in onDraw, which runs whenever a monitor draws the script and can run several times when one script drives several monitors. Composite functions do nothing in onDraw. The shipped example reads number channels 3 and 4 and boolean channel 1 in onTick and draws the matching rectangle in onDraw.

sections.title: Wiring
sections.body: Feed Video Signal from a microcontroller or camera, connect Electric and turn Power Switch on. For a touchscreen, wire Touch Output to a composite input on the microcontroller that draws the screen and its video output back to Video Signal. While the screen is switched off, every Touch Output channel reads 0.

families.summary: Pumps heat from liquid A to liquid B by a fixed amount per update, even against the gradient, while powered and switched on.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Case 0x21 pumps only with On/Off on, electricity supplied above 0.1 of the request, and the two compartments together holding more than 0.001 capacity units. Each update it requests 0.001 electricity units, 0.06 per simulated second.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: Unlike an exchanger it does not stop at equal temperatures: A loses 0.03·qB/(qA+qB) and B gains 0.03·qA/(qA+qB) every update, so B can be driven hotter than A. While q stays constant, that is 1.8·qB/(qA+qB) and 1.8·qA/(qA+qB) per simulated second. Remove heat from B with a radiator or exchanger or the transfer stalls as B climbs.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Electric unit cost of the 0.001 request and the capacity terms q per litre of each liquid.

families.summary: Belt-driven pump coupled to the crank by clutch pressure; its own speed decays by the factor 0.99 every update.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: The fluid-pump case couples the pump speed to the crank weighted by its engine_max_force (0.5) against the crank inertia, scaled by Clutch Pressure clamped between zero and one, then pumps and multiplies its speed by 0.99. Uncoupled, it keeps 0.547 of its speed after one simulated second (time constant 1.66 s).

sections.title: Flow
sections.body: The pump pushes with a bias equal to its own shaft speed in RPS and is one-way. At equal pressure it moves at most 20 L/s per RPS, reaching the 400 L/s bound at 20 RPS. Its speed is not crank RPS × clutch: it moves toward the belt speed by the clutch and inertia share each update and is then multiplied by 0.99. Without a belt group, or when damaged, it passes fluid only where pressure already pushes it. Its pump_pressure field is not read.

findings.label: Ticks per simulated second
findings.detail: The worker converts its tick count (worker+0xd0, loaded at 0x1405e3ad7) to binary32 and divides it by this, then passes the widened result as the elapsed time to the physics world's stepSimulation slot +0x60 at 0x1405e3b16, with at most 1000 solver substeps. With tick count 1 the elapsed simulated time is 1/60 s. Report: investigation/update-rate.md. findings.label: Solver substep
findings.value: 1 ÷ solver rate
findings.detail: The substep is 1 ÷ the worker's solver rate (worker+0xb8), or binary32 1/60 from 0x140baf98c in the fallback branch at 0x1405e3af4. The accumulator 0x140133ea0 runs whole substeps of that length. The component dispatch is outside that loop, so the solver rates 60, 120 and 180 chosen by the coordinator do not multiply component updates. Report: investigation/update-rate.md. families.summary: Anchors only within about 1 m of terrain and ±30 degrees of upright; unanchoring resets drilling progress.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Drive the rod from a rotary table, force it down and keep drilling slurry flowing through a swivel; extract saturated slurry from the well head.

findings.label: Oil Rig Well Head · tooltip
findings.value: Once anchored to the terrain, a drill rod can be inserted into a well head to begin drilling a well. In order to drill effectively a drill rod should be driven by a rotary table and forced downward toward the terrain. A continuous supply of drilling slurry must be provided through the drill rod via a swivel, and the saturated drilling slurry extracted from the well head fluid port.
findings.detail: oil_rig_well_head: developer-authored description; intended behaviour, not a measurement.

findings.label: Oil Rig Well Head · port Anchor
findings.value: Extend / retract piles to anchor the well head to the terrain, allowing for a new well to be drilled. The well head must be close to the terrain (~1m) and upright (+-30 degrees) to be anchored. Unanchoring the well will reset any drilling progress made.
findings.detail: oil_rig_well_head: input port. Interface description.

families.summary: Deploys on signal, opens at 20 m/s, stalls below 5 m/s, and must be refolded at a workbench after use.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Hold Deploy on; it closes when the signal stops or it stalls. Size is set with the select tool.

findings.label: Vehicle Parachute · tooltip
findings.value: The parachute will deploy when receiving an on signal, and will close when not. Once deployed, it will open at a speed of 20m/s and stall when it drops below 5m/s. Once opened, the single use will be consumed and it must be returned to a workbench to be refolded. The size of the parachute can be customised by selecting this component with the select tool.
findings.detail: parachute: developer-authored description; intended behaviour, not a measurement.

findings.label: Vehicle Parachute · port Deploy
findings.value: Deploy the parachute. The parachute will close when it stalls or stops receiving an on signal.
findings.detail: parachute: input port. Interface description.

families.summary: Seventeen composite channels of position, rotation and velocity; GPS position needs electricity.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Channels 1–3 position, 4–6 Euler rotation, 7–9 linear and 10 to 12 angular velocity, 13–14 absolute speeds, 15–16 local tilts and 17 compass heading from −0.5 to 0.5. It measures along its local Y axis.

findings.label: Physics Sensor · tooltip
findings.value: Outputs physics information to a composite logic node. Requires Electric for GPS position functionality. This component is directed along its local Y axis.
findings.detail: physics_sensor: developer-authored description; intended behaviour, not a measurement.

findings.label: Physics Sensor · port Composite Output
findings.value: Outputs [1] x position, [2] y position, [3] z position, [4] euler rotation x, [5] euler rotation y, [6] euler rotation z, [7] linear velocity x, [8] linear velocity y, [9] linear velocity z, [10] angular velocity x, [11] angular velocity y, [12] angular velocity z, [13] absolute linear velocity, [14] absolute angular velocity, [15] local z tilt, [16] local x tilt and [17] compass heading (-0.5 to 0.5) to the respective composite channels.

families.summary: Takes outside air through its Fluid port. Airspeed in m/s along the part's local +X axis, the side the mouth faces, adds 0.1 × speed of bias, which acts like 2 × that much extra outside pressure; inside an enclosed compartment it is a plain port.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Case 0xf shares the fluid-update block of cases 0, 0xc and 0x17, which does nothing until the Fluid port is connected. Each update 0x140311f20 builds the state outside the port. If the scoop sits in an enclosed compartment, outside means that compartment's air, the factor is 1 and no speed term is added. Otherwise the outside is fresh air when the port is above the water surface and sea water when it is below.

sections.title: Outside pressure
sections.body:
Air pressure is (1 - 2.2413793e-05 × y)^5.3595023 with y the port's world height in metres, 1 at sea level, 0.8856 at 1000 m, 0.5289 at 5000 m and 0.2566 at 10000 m. Above 40000 m it is 0. The air is 20 units split 15.792, 4.2 and 0.007999999 across fluid indices 11, 10 and 4, the dry-air nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide shares, though the code does not name them.

Under water the pressure is 30 - 29 ÷ (1 + 0.001 × depth): 1.2871 at 10 m, 3.6364 at 100 m, 15.5 at 1000 m. The outside fluid is 20 units of index 6 plus any oil the world map holds at that spot, so a submerged scoop pulls water.

sections.title: Speed term
sections.body:
The update takes the port's velocity, including spin, subtracts the wind and projects the result on the part's local X axis. The mesh mouth faces local +X, so driving mouth first in still air gives a positive speed; air entering the mouth moves along -X. Speed is in m/s: the linear speed sensor, whose output is documented in m/s, uses the same velocity calculation without conversion.

Bias = 0.1 × voxel count × that speed, clamped to -10…10; the scoop has 1 voxel, so the clamp is hit at 100 m/s. Moving tail first gives a negative bias that favors outflow from the network, and sideways motion adds nothing.

sections.title: Wind
sections.body: The subtracted vector is the vehicle's cached weather wind, so the scoop responds to airspeed rather than ground speed. Facing into a headwind raises the bias, and a tailwind as fast as the vehicle cancels it. The game samples the wind once per vehicle at its transformed origin, not at each scoop. The sample includes local weather-cell wind and is scaled by 1 - shelter, so inside a weather shelter volume it is 0. A vehicle whose parent-body link (vehicle+0x14b8) is set gets zero wind on this path.

sections.title: Flow per update and per second
sections.body:
The port routine works in pressure units where 1 is sea-level air. For a gas-filled pipe network of 8 or more volume units, away from the target-pressure and free-window clamps, the demand is (P_net - (p_out + 2 × bias)) ÷ 15 amount per update, negative meaning inflow, and inflow demand stops growing at 2 ÷ 15 × p_out. The move magnitude is at most 0.5 × factor × the absolute demand, using the network's allocation from the previous update. At exactly P_net - p_out - bias = 0 the routine instead sets demand to 0.

At sea level with the network at pressure 1, a sole scoop moves 0.0167, 0.0333, 0.05 and 0.0667 amount per update at 2.5, 5, 7.5 and 10 m/s, and stays at 0.0667 above that. The port counter stores 600 × the gas amount moved in one update (10, 20, 30 and 40), and the inspection tooltip multiplies it by 60 and shows L/s: 600, 1200, 1800 and 2400 L/s. A stationary scoop on a network an engine has pulled to 0 moves 0.0333 amount per update, 1200 L/s, so speed can double the best static intake. At altitude the maximum inflow scales with p_out while the bias does not. Unsaturated flow does not generally scale in the same way; it depends on network pressure too.

Component updates run 60 times per simulated second, so under the same assumptions the sea-level cap is 4 amount per second, shown as 2400 L/s. The still scoop into a network at 0 takes 2 amount per second (1200 L/s), and below the cap flow into a network at 1 is 0.4 × speed amount per second, 240 × speed L/s up to 10 m/s. The tooltip therefore counts 1 gas amount as 600 L. That factor is fixed and does not divide by network pressure, so the figure is not the compressed volume in the pipes. These are rates at a fixed state; a filling network raises P_net and the flow falls.

sections.title: Near volcanoes
sections.body: In air, the move is also scaled by an exchange factor. Volcanoes lower it: each active volcano adds a source with strength volcanic_heat² and radius 0.5 × eruption_radius at its position. The factor is max(0.01, 1 - volcanic_heat² × eruption_radius ÷ (2 × distance)) for the strongest source, so a hot volcano with a wide eruption radius can cut intake to 0.01 of normal near it. Away from volcanoes the factor is 1. Under water it stays 1.

sections.title: Sealed network
sections.body: The simplified demand has a zero at P_net = p_out + 2 × bias: 3 at 10 m/s, 11 at 50 and 21 at 100 or more, where the bias clamp caps it. The exact branch also gives zero demand at P_net = p_out + bias. These are mathematical zero-demand points, not a verified final pressure for a filling network.

findings.value: demand = (P_net - (p_out + 2 × bias)) ÷ 15, inflow ≤ 2 ÷ 15 × p_out

Function 0x1405e8fb0-0x1405ec4a4; instruction bytes e8dfd4f5ff at 0x1405ebd5c. Interpretation rests on retained output investigation/native/behavior/../update-rate/asm/stormworks64-scene-dispatch.asm:L31. Provenance: Ghidra 12.1.4 headless, program imported with -noanalysis and only the cited routine disassembled/decompiled by a local script; this is not an REA session record. Static analysis of this executable only; no game process was run.

findings.label: Component update call
findings.value: one call per component
findings.detail: The dispatcher clears its component index at 0x1405497be, makes one call through vtable slot +0x358 per iteration and increments the index at 0x1405498dd. Slot +0x358 holds 0x1403ef860 in the water component vtable (0x140b09270), 0x1404008a0 in the electric one (0x140b81428) and 0x140449670 in the modular-engine one (0x140b9cc08); the extractor re-reads those three pointers. Report: investigation/update-rate.md. Function 0x140549240-0x140549ef6; instruction bytes 41ff9258030000 at 0x1405498d6. Interpretation rests on retained output investigation/native/behavior/../update-rate/asm/stormworks64-component-dispatch.asm:L55-L110; ../update-rate/tables.txt:L7-L12. Provenance: Ghidra 12.1.4 headless, program imported with -noanalysis and only the cited routine disassembled/decompiled by a local script; this is not an REA session record. Static analysis of this executable only; no game process was run.

findings.label: Physics ticks per component pass
findings.detail: After the component pass the coordinator stores 1 at scene+0x6788 (worker+0xd0) and submits the scene physics worker (update_thread_task@c_scene) at 0x1407439df. One component pass therefore corresponds to one physics tick. Report: investigation/update-rate.md. Function 0x14073f890-0x1407468e3; instruction bytes b801000000898288670000 at 0x1407439c6. Interpretation rests on retained output investigation/native/behavior/../update-rate/asm/stormworks64-physics-submit.asm:L139-L148; ../update-rate/asm/stormworks64-physics-construction.asm. Provenance: Ghidra 12.1.4 headless, program imported with -noanalysis and only the cited routine disassembled/decompiled by a local script; this is not an REA session record. Static analysis of this executable only; no game process was run.

findings.label: Ticks per simulated second
findings.detail: The worker converts its tick count (worker+0xd0, loaded at 0x1405e3ad7) to binary32 and divides it by this, then passes the widened result as the elapsed time to the physics world's stepSimulation slot +0x60 at 0x1405e3b16, with at most 1000 solver substeps. With tick count 1 the elapsed simulated time is 1/60 s. Report: investigation/update-rate.md. Function 0x1405e3a80-0x1405e3b4d; instruction bytes f30f5e0d6ecc5c00 at 0x1405e3aea address binary32 60 (bytes 00007042) at 0x140bb0760. Interpretation rests on retained output investigation/native/behavior/../update-rate/asm/stormworks64-physics-worker.asm:L19-L31; ../update-rate/pseudocode/0x1405e3a80.c; ../update-rate/tables.txt:L4,L13-L14. Provenance: Ghidra 12.1.4 headless, program imported with -noanalysis and only the cited routine disassembled/decompiled by a local script; this is not an REA session record. Static analysis of this executable only; no game process was run.

findings.label: Solver substep
findings.value: 1 ÷ solver rate
findings.detail: The substep is 1 ÷ the worker's solver rate (worker+0xb8), or binary32 1/60 from 0x140baf98c in the fallback branch at 0x1405e3af4. The accumulator 0x140133ea0 runs whole substeps of that length. The component dispatch is outside that loop, so the solver rates 60, 120 and 180 chosen by the coordinator do not multiply component updates. Report: investigation/update-rate.md. Function 0x1405e3a80-0x1405e3b4d; instruction bytes f30f5e83b8000000 at 0x1405e3add. Interpretation rests on retained output investigation/native/behavior/../update-rate/asm/stormworks64-physics-worker.asm:L20-L31; ../update-rate/asm/stormworks64-physics-accumulator.asm. Provenance: Ghidra 12.1.4 headless, program imported with -noanalysis and only the cited routine disassembled/decompiled by a local script; this is not an REA session record. Static analysis of this executable only; no game process was run.

limitations: Static decompilation of one build; the game was not run and no flow was measured.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

The flow figures assume the scoop is the only port moving gas into a network of at least 8 volume units with room to spare. With several ports, the allocation gives each f·|f| ÷ Σ|f|, and the move lags the demand by one update.
Volcanoes are the producer of exchange-factor sources found in this build. The search identified that writer but did not exhaustively exclude every other writer to the list.
The L/s figure on the inspection tooltip is a fixed display factor of 600 L per gas amount. It does not measure the compressed gas volume in the network.
